entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of “When Forgetting is not Catastrophic”

link.title: Rewriting the abstract of “When Forgetting is not Catastrophic”

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract makes you wait for its point. The claim that forgetting is two processes, and only one is catastrophic, arrives in the second-to-last sentence. It also describes the mechanism in the vocabulary of its toy model (“keys with shared structure, concentrated new values”) before saying what those words mean. The rewrite opens with the two processes, gives the evidence next, and turns the toy-model terms into plain conditions.

Before and after

Before Knowledge that a language model appears to forget during finetuning often remains stored and can be recovered, a phenomenon called spurious forgetting. Finetuning on new facts can even produce forgetting that undoes itself: recall of the old facts collapses, recovers as training continues on new facts alone, and only then erodes for good. We seek to understand when such forgetting is not catastrophic. A minimal associative memory reproduces these dynamics with three ingredients: keys with shared structure, concentrated new values, and normalization in the network. Finetuning moves all old representations along a common direction, hiding the old facts while preserving their relative geometry; normalization withdraws this shift once the new facts are learned, whereas fact-specific changes accumulate and cause the erosion. Moreover, subtracting the common shift eliminates the collapse in a Transformer trained on synthetic data, and removing a single direction from each weight update restores old facts in a pretrained language model. Forgetting thus combines a shared, reversible loss of access with a slow erosion of individual facts, and only the second is catastrophic. Which one dominates depends on whether the new data move old memories together or apart.
After Forgetting during finetuning is not one process but two: a fast, shared loss of access that can reverse on its own, and a slow erosion of individual facts that cannot. We see both when a model is finetuned on new facts alone: recall of old facts collapses, comes back as training continues, and only then erodes for good. The collapse happens because finetuning moves all old representations along a common direction; normalization withdraws this shift once the new facts are learned, while fact-specific changes accumulate and cause the erosion. A minimal model shows that this requires three things: facts queried in similar ways, new answers concentrated in one part of the vocabulary, and a normalization layer. We confirm this causally: subtracting the common shift removes the collapse in a Transformer trained on synthetic biographies, and removing a single direction from each weight update restores old facts in a pretrained language model. Only the slow erosion is catastrophic, and which process dominates depends on whether the new data move old memories together or apart.

The general rule

Put the finding in the first sentence. Then describe the conditions in the reader’s terms, not your model’s.
entry.summary: Forgetting during finetuning is two processes, and only one is permanent. The rewritten abstract says so in its first sentence.

entry.title: A better Figure 5
entry.content:
The original

Figure 5 fine-tunes OLMo 2 1B on new facts only (no replay) and checks the old facts it already knew. It has three panels, one per analysis: old and new facts for both runs (left), old facts with the top singular direction of each weight update removed (middle), and a small vs. large set of new individuals (right).

What makes it hard to read:

  • The panels are organized by analysis, so one run is spread over three panels and you compare by eye.
  • The middle panel shows old facts only, so the edit looks like a pure win. Its cost on the new facts is not shown.
  • Line shades change between panels (navy, red, pink, gray) and the legends differ in each one.

The redesign

What changed and why

  • One panel per run (synthetic individuals, real entities, large set).
  • Same color means the same thing in every panel: blue is old facts, green is old facts with the top direction removed, gray dashed is new facts.
  • The edit sits next to normal training in the same panel, so its effect on old facts is one comparison.
  • One shared legend under the plots, and no labels on the plot. The one-line hint for each run is in the caption.
  • The large set gets its own panel with old and new facts only, since the paper does not report the edit for it.
  • The original shows the edit only helping old facts. The redesign adds its cost on the new facts, from Table 3: a gray hollow star at step 400 in each run. For synthetic individuals, new-fact accuracy drops from 0.90 to 0.40, and for real entities, from 1.00 to 0.66. Only step 400 is drawn; the step 80 values (0.03 to 0.01 and 0.46 to 0.25) are in the table.
entry.summary: One panel per run, so you can see what removing the top direction does to old facts and what it costs on new facts.

entry.title: Reproducing Spurious Forgetting: Shared Keys Hide Old Facts

link.title: Reproducing Spurious Forgetting: Shared Keys Hide Old Facts

entry.content:
What I reimplemented

I reproduced Figure 2, panel 1 from When Forgetting is Not Catastrophic: On the Mechanics of Spurious Forgetting.

The experiment studies how sharing structure between fact keys changes forgetting:

\[k_i = \sqrt{\alpha}\,\mu + \sqrt{1-\alpha}\,e_i,\]

where $\mu$ is shared by all facts and $e_i$ belongs only to fact $i$. A larger $\alpha$ means that different facts look more alike to the model.

I used the paper’s setup: dimension 128, 32 output tokens, and 128 facts in each set. The model first learned old facts $A$ and $B$, then trained for 500 steps only on new facts $B’$. I measured accuracy on $A$ throughout, without replay, and averaged ten seeds.

The code

The implementation is a small NumPy version of the paper’s associative memory. This is the core of the experiment:

# Build keys with a shared part and a fact-specific part.
keys = np.sqrt(alpha) * mu + np.sqrt(1 - alpha) * own_vectors

# Two linear layers with RMS normalization between them.
h = keys @ w1.T
x = np.sqrt(d) * h / np.linalg.norm(h, axis=1, keepdims=True)
probs = softmax(x @ w2.T)

I used a pretraining learning rate of 0.1. A one-seed pilot gave a fine-tuning rate of 0.02, which made the new facts reach 0.99 accuracy around step 200 as described in the paper.

  • Full reproduction script
  • Requirements
  • Per-seed curves
  • Mean and standard-deviation curves
  • Run metadata

To rerun it:

cd assets/code/spurious-forgetting-figure2-panel1
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python reproduce.py \
  --seeds 0-9 \
  --out-dir ../../data/spurious-forgetting-figure2-panel1
cp ../../data/spurious-forgetting-figure2-panel1/figure2_panel1.svg \
  ../../img/posts/coding-nathan/figure2-panel1.svg

Results

$\alpha$ Mean accuracy at step 0 Trough (step, accuracy) Step 200 Step 500
0 0.995 (498, 0.565) 0.806 0.565
0.1 0.996 (500, 0.266) 0.449 0.266
0.25 0.997 (497, 0.261) 0.319 0.261
0.5 0.996 (74, 0.118) 0.390 0.334

At $\alpha=0$, forgetting is gradual. At $\alpha=0.5$, accuracy quickly falls from 0.996 to 0.118, recovers to about 0.40, and then slowly declines again.

The shared part of the keys makes updates to $B’$ move many old representations in the same direction. This temporarily hides the old answers. As the model learns the individual new facts, RMS normalization helps undo part of that shared movement, so some old accuracy returns. The later decline comes from smaller fact-specific changes that are not undone.

Comparison with the paper

The main pattern matches the paper: stronger sharing gives a faster collapse, while $\alpha=0$ gives ordinary gradual forgetting. The $\alpha=0.5$ curve also shows the expected recovery and later erosion.

The numbers are not an exact match. My recovery peaks around 0.40, and the intermediate curves end somewhat lower. The paper does not report all initialization and learning-rate details for this toy experiment, which could explain the difference.

I could inspect the official repository, but this environment could not clone or download its toy/ files. The code here therefore follows the published equations rather than running the authors’ JAX implementation.

What I learned

The main takeaway for me is that low accuracy does not always mean the information was erased. With shared keys, the model can temporarily lose access to many facts at once and later recover them without seeing them again.

It was also useful to plot the full training trajectory. If I had measured only near step 74, I would have concluded that almost everything was forgotten. The recovery shows why that conclusion would be too strong.

entry.title: Redo Graph Spurious Forgetting 9xtc
entry.content:
title: “A better Figure 5” description: “Removing one direction restores forgotten facts: a direct comparison of old-fact recall before and after the intervention.” paper: spurious-forgetting task: redo-graph by: [golombi] chart: chartjs: true —

The original

Figure 5 in the original paper

Figure 5 (middle) shows that removing the top singular direction of each weight update during finetuning can restore the model’s ability to recall old facts.

The authors compare the original finetuned model with a model whose updates have their top singular direction removed. They also compare against removing a random direction as a control.

The problem is that the figure uses continuous curves, making it difficult to compare the exact improvement between methods. Readers must estimate the distance between curves and mentally calculate how much old-fact recall was recovered.

The most important result is not immediately obvious: removing a single direction can recover a large fraction of the apparently forgotten knowledge, while removing a random direction has almost no effect.

The redesign

Instead of continuous curves, I use grouped bars to directly compare old-fact recall under the three conditions at two meaningful checkpoints.

The values come from Table 3 of the paper, which reports accuracy at step 80 (the trough) and step 400 for two types of new facts.

{
  "type": "bar",
  "data": {
    "labels": [
      ["Synthetic facts", "Step 80"],
      ["Synthetic facts", "Step 400"],
      ["Real entities", "Step 80"],
      ["Real entities", "Step 400"]
    ],
    "datasets": [
      {
        "label": "Original finetuning",
        "data": [28, 38, 73, 55],
        "backgroundColor": "#E76F51",
        "borderRadius": 4
      },
      {
        "label": "Top direction removed",
        "data": [77, 70, 88, 79],
        "backgroundColor": "#2A9D8F",
        "borderRadius": 4
      },
      {
        "label": "Random direction removed",
        "data": [28, 38, 73, 55],
        "backgroundColor": "#A8ADB5",
        "borderRadius": 4
      }
    ]
  },
  "options": {
    "responsive": true,
    "plugins": {
      "title": {
        "display": true,
        "text": "Removing One Direction Restores Forgotten Facts",
        "font": {
          "size": 18,
          "weight": "bold"
        },
        "padding": {
          "bottom": 18
        }
      },
      "subtitle": {
        "display": true,
        "text": "Old-fact recall (%) — higher is better",
        "padding": {
          "bottom": 15
        }
      },
      "legend": {
        "position": "bottom"
      },
      "tooltip": {
        "callbacks": {
          "label": "function(context) { return context.dataset.label + ': ' + context.parsed.y + '%'; }"
        }
      }
    },
    "scales": {
      "y": {
        "beginAtZero": true,
        "max": 100,
        "title": {
          "display": true,
          "text": "Old-fact recall (%)"
        },
        "ticks": {
          "stepSize": 20
        }
      },
      "x": {
        "grid": {
          "display": false
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Main takeaway: At step 80, removing the top direction increases old-fact recall from 28% to 77% for synthetic facts, a gain of 49 percentage points. Removing a random direction produces no improvement.

The same intervention also improves recall for real entities, suggesting that some apparently forgotten knowledge remains accessible when the harmful update direction is removed.

Caption: Old-fact recall in OLMo 2 1B under three finetuning conditions. Bars show the reported mean accuracies at steps 80 and 400, using values from Table 3. The top-direction intervention restores substantial old-fact recall, unlike the random-direction control. The intervention also reduces new-fact learning accuracy, a tradeoff not shown here.

What changed and why

  • Replaced curves with grouped bars: Makes the differences between interventions visible without requiring the reader to estimate distances between lines.
  • Selected two meaningful checkpoints: Step 80 captures the collapse, while step 400 shows whether the improvement persists later in training.
  • Used consistent colors: Red represents ordinary finetuning, green represents the proposed intervention, and gray represents the random-direction control.
  • Used percentages instead of decimals: Makes accuracy easier to interpret immediately.
  • Kept the random-direction control: Shows that the improvement is specific to the top direction, rather than simply removing any direction.
  • Included both types of new facts: Shows that the intervention helps for both synthetic individuals and real entities.
  • Focused on old-fact recall: Removes distracting information so the reader can immediately understand the paper’s central finding about recoverable forgetting.

The redesigned figure emphasizes the distinction between knowledge being destroyed and knowledge becoming temporarily inaccessible, which is the central idea of the paper.

entry.title: The authors’ path: Spurious forgetting
entry.content:
Vedant Palit

Vedant Palit is a machine learning researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, collaborating with Zhijing Jin’s research group at the University of Toronto. His research focuses on mechanistic interpretability, particularly understanding how language models and vision-language models represent and process information internally. His previous work includes developing causal tracing methods for multimodal models and investigating the internal circuits responsible for learned concepts and reasoning.

When Forgetting is not Catastrophic fits directly into his research interests by investigating the internal mechanisms responsible for forgetting in language models. Rather than treating forgetting solely as a loss of learned knowledge, the paper examines how changes in internal representations can temporarily prevent models from accessing information that remains stored. This builds on his broader interest in understanding model behavior through mechanistic analysis and identifying how internal representations influence performance.

Florent Draye

Florent Draye is a PhD researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, supervised by Bernhard Schölkopf. His research focuses on mechanistic interpretability, representation learning, and causal structures in neural networks. He is particularly interested in understanding the internal representations learned by large language models, including their world models and how these representations change through training. His work also includes developing tools for analyzing neural circuits and investigating how interpretable features emerge within models.

When Forgetting is not Catastrophic connects closely to his research on representation learning and mechanistic interpretability. The paper investigates how fine-tuning changes the internal representations of previously learned facts and distinguishes between temporary shifts that make knowledge inaccessible and changes that permanently damage stored information. This aligns with his broader goal of understanding how neural networks organize information and how their internal representations affect model behavior.

Nicolas Zucchet

Nicolas Zucchet is a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford University whose work focuses on machine learning, computational neuroscience, and neural network learning dynamics. He previously completed his PhD at ETH Zürich and conducted research at Google DeepMind. His research investigates how neural networks learn, store, and organize information, including how training data and learning curricula influence model behavior. His previous work includes studying how language models acquire factual knowledge, how attention mechanisms emerge, and how different learning strategies affect neural networks.

When Forgetting is not Catastrophic is closely related to his previous research on how language models learn facts. In particular, his paper How Do Language Models Learn Facts? Dynamics, Curricula and Hallucinations studies how factual knowledge is acquired during training. The new paper extends this line of investigation by examining what happens to previously learned facts when models are trained on new information. Both works seek to understand the learning dynamics underlying factual knowledge rather than evaluating models only through their final performance.

Zhijing Jin

Zhijing Jin is an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Toronto and a research scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems. Her research focuses on large language models, causal inference, mechanistic interpretability, and AI safety. She is particularly interested in understanding how language models reason, how their internal representations influence behavior, and how causal methods can help explain and improve their capabilities. Her previous work includes developing benchmarks for causal reasoning and investigating the mechanisms underlying model behavior.

When Forgetting is not Catastrophic aligns with her research through its use of mechanistic analysis to explain language model behavior. The paper moves beyond observing that fine-tuning causes forgetting and instead investigates the representational changes responsible for this behavior. By identifying mechanisms that distinguish reversible forgetting from genuine knowledge loss, the work connects to her broader interest in explaining model behavior through internal representations and causal interventions.

Bernhard Schölkopf

Bernhard Schölkopf is a prominent machine learning researcher and director of the Empirical Inference Department at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems. His research has made significant contributions to statistical learning theory, kernel methods, and causal inference. More recently, his work has emphasized causal representation learning, which aims to understand how models can discover meaningful underlying structures in data rather than relying only on statistical correlations. His broader research seeks to improve the interpretability, robustness, and generalization capabilities of machine learning systems.

When Forgetting is not Catastrophic connects to his research on representation learning and the mechanisms underlying neural network behavior. The paper shows that apparent forgetting can arise from shared shifts in learned representations without necessarily destroying the information they encode. This distinction relates to his broader interest in understanding how learned representations influence model behavior and generalization. By developing a simplified mathematical model and testing its predictions through interventions, the work also reflects his emphasis on explaining machine learning phenomena through underlying mechanisms rather than observations alone.
entry.summary: How the authors’ research on mechanistic interpretability, representation learning, and learning dynamics connects to spurious forgetting.

entry.title: The authors’ path
entry.content:
Vedant Palit works on mechanistic interpretability, studying how computations inside a model shape its answers. In a 2023 study of BLIP (a vision-language model), he and his coauthors traced how the model used information from an image to answer a question. In How Do Linear Probes Emerge?, Palit explored a related question: which computations make a concept detectable inside a language model even when its answer never mentions it? The current paper brings that question to memory. When a model stops recalling a fact after fine-tuning, how can we tell whether it still retains that knowledge?

Bernhard Schölkopf is a machine learning researcher known for his work on kernel methods. He has also studied causal inference, particularly how to uncover the mechanisms behind patterns in data. His recent work on mechanistic interpretability with Palit brings that causal perspective to language models. By changing specific parts of a model’s computation and observing the effect, they investigate which internal mechanisms explain its behavior.
entry.summary: How Vedant Palit’s work on interpretability and Bernhard Schölkopf’s research on causality connect to spurious forgetting.

entry.title: Critique of Spurious Forgetting paper
entry.content:
This paper deals with an intriguing phenomena related to a common failure mode for large neural models (lagnuage models or others). Fine tuning is known to hurt capabilities in already-learend tasks. The phenomena described here, named “Spurious forgetting”, deals with cases in which the original capabilities, namely information that was originally stored in the model, is still recoverable after forgetting.

The paper tries to give an answer as to HOW This happens, and builds an interseting mathematical model that explains it.

Strengths.

  • Writing - it is well written. most sections provide, in my opionion, a clean and well seperated idea that one could understand. It is not overly simplified, but it maintains good balance between making the ideas accessible while not underselling the complexity.

  • Mathematical model - the mathematical ideas that are suggested in the paper, namely the geometric representation of old and new facts during training, the effects of normalization, and the ingredients needed to replicate the phenomena - seemed all well established to me. Under the assumptions of the paper, they offer a plausible and intuitive explanation of the failure mode that causes this phenomena.

Weaknesses

  • Representability - the assumed minimal model seems somewhat different from the way an actual LLM functions:
    1. The minimal model focuses only on MLP layers while abstracting attention. this might be a logical step, but a clearer link to a full attention head would be closer to a real LLM.
    2. The structure of the keys in the toy model, seems overly simplified - they introduce one shared direction component and another random direction component. This assumption should be emprically checked in a real LLM, not assumed.
    3. fixed keys in the geometry - this entirely ignores the fact that earlier layers are also trained simoltaniously, which may cause the keys themselves to shift during training.
  • Generality of results - while the experiments overall are interesting, they don’t fully control for all variables, and may fail to represent a real case of Fine Tuning:
    1. Synthetic biographies are somewhat biased- Tthey are in fact favorable to the proposed mechanism. In Section 4.1, shared templates encourage similar query representations, and the answer pools are partitioned so that new facts use answers outside population (A)’s pool.
    2. The OLMo experiment still enforces answer separation, a key assumption in the toy model: new answers cannot share their first token with old answers. The synthetic and real datasets also differ in several ways, so the comparison does not isolate subject–answer predictability as the cause of recovery.
    3. The collapse/recovery/erosion curve seen in Figure 1 is only based on a single pretrained model. this behaviourm ay be differnet for other models.

Overall, the paper offers an intuitive explanation with convincing evidence for controlled settings. The main question, in my opinion, is whether the same mechanism explains forgetting during more realistic LLM finetuning cases. The OLMo experiment is a useful step, but its restrictions does not fully answer the question.
entry.summary: The Spurious Forgetting paper offers a cool and intuitive explanation of this odd phenomena, but assumes rather strong assumptions that might not be reproducible or hold for real-sized LLMs.

entry.title: Literature review: where spurious forgetting comes from

link.title: Literature review: where spurious forgetting comes from

entry.content:
I read the paper’s introduction, discussion and reference list, plus the arXiv abstracts of eight cited papers (the ones with links). For the rest I only know what the paper says about them. I ran no code.

The papers this builds on

The problem: catastrophic forgetting. Training on new data damages old knowledge: classic reports (McCloskey & Cohen 1989, French 1999), deep networks (Goodfellow et al. 2014, Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) and language models (Luo et al. 2025, Zucchet et al. 2025). The paper says part of this is something else.

The direct ancestors: a drop in performance is not a loss of knowledge.

  • Zheng et al. 2025 coined “spurious forgetting”: performance drops often reflect lost task alignment, linked to orthogonal weight updates. The new paper looks for a mechanism instead (a common shift of representations that normalization later withdraws) and only suggests it may be a concrete form of Zheng et al.’s task-alignment loss.
  • Kotha et al. 2024: fine-tuning skews which task the model infers from a prompt, and a changed prompt recovers some capability. The new paper’s recovery needs no special prompt, probe or replay.
  • De Lange et al. 2023, the “stability gap”: performance drops after a new task starts, then recovers. This is the same curve shape, but the paper cites it in one sentence only (my observation). The setting differs: they study continual-learning methods, the paper studies plain fine-tuning without replay.
  • Shallow forgetting (Murata et al. 2020, Davari et al. 2022, Hess et al. 2024, Lanzillotta et al. 2026): old information stays linearly decodable even when outputs fail. The paper’s “hidden, not erased” is this idea for individual facts.
  • Older roots, as the paper describes them: stored versus accessible memory in psychology (Tulving & Pearlstone 1966) and recovery of forgotten associations in connectionist networks (Hinton & Plaut 1987, Atkins & Murre 1998).

How a model stores a fact (the setup). Feed-forward layers as key-value memories (Geva et al. 2021); Meng et al. 2022 show facts are localized and editable with rank-one updates, and their CounterFact set supplies the old facts for the pretrained-model test. The controlled synthetic biographies come from Allen-Zhu & Li 2024. Zucchet et al. 2025 find that fine-tuning on new facts “quickly corrupts” existing ones, which is closely related to the question here (my reading, not stated by the paper).

What changes how much is forgotten. Larger learning rates mean more forgetting (Gupta et al. 2023, Ibrahim et al. 2024, Lin et al. 2026, Rofin et al. 2026), and Springer et al. 2025 show that longer-pretrained models can be harder to fine-tune. The paper finds its collapse deepens with the learning rate and concludes part of that effect is spurious.

The concepts it connects to

Concept Role in this paper
Catastrophic forgetting The phenomenon it splits in two
Availability vs. accessibility (psychology) The old idea behind “hidden, not erased”
Shallow vs. deep forgetting Evidence that old information survives in representations
Stability gap A forgetting curve of the same shape
Factual recall as associative memory The minimal model and the synthetic setup
Normalization layers Usually stabilizers; here they withdraw the shift and cause recovery
Shared structure is learned first (Saxe et al. 2019) Explains why the shift reverses only slowly
Rank-one weight edits The fix removes one direction of each update; the link to editing is my observation

Read first, and what I’m unsure about

Read Zheng et al. 2025 (the phenomenon), De Lange et al. 2023 (the same curve elsewhere) and Zucchet et al. 2025 (the data and dynamics).

Open questions: is the paper’s common shift the same thing as Zheng et al.’s orthogonal update (the paper only says “may be”)? Where does it stand relative to the stability gap? And of the 2026 references I checked only Lanzillotta et al.

Paper: arXiv:2610.08718.
entry.summary: The paper sits where four lines of work meet: catastrophic forgetting, forgetting that is actually recoverable, factual recall as associative memory, and what training choices change how much is forgotten.

entry.title: Week 4 in one page: all about Tokenization

link.title: Week 4 in one page: all about Tokenization

entry.content:
About the paper

This week we dove into tokenization through a survey that works on two levels: a high-level map of the field, and a detailed reference for those who want to go deeper. Text is both the input and the output of an LLM, but before a model can process it, the text has to be split into tokens and converted into numerical values. Although this step is central, and is behind popular failures like miscounting the r’s in “strawberry”, it rarely gets the spotlight. The 32 authors aim to bring it to the surface, covering algorithms, multilingual challenges, evaluation, theory and more.

Our posts:

✍️ Writing. Rewriting the abstract skips some background and jumps right ahead to why we should care about the topic. Our beginner-friendly copy edits suggested some context for the Unigram algorithm in the Tokenization Algorithms section (3), explaining what it means to assign tokens probabilities, and a simplified opening of 4.1 normalization in the Pretokenization section. This is a long survey, so we send you home with key points through a TL;DR: Tokenizers can be compared, updated without retraining from scratch, and if you learn only one algorithm, make it BPE.

🧠 Learning. One of the reasons tokenization matters: security. It is also the barrier between the model and natural language, leading to some of the popular failures. To work through BPE, we introduce it first intuitively, using an example. More on BPE later.

📊 Visualization. We visualize the numbers behind the significance of tokenization research: how much of a model’s parameters the vocabulary takes up, and, in contrast, how little spotlight the topic gets. Expanding on the overview in Figure 1.1, we emphasize the many-to-one probability mapping of token sequences to a sentence. Diving into token allocation bias between languages, a revisited Figure 6.1 highlights English as the reference and compares different tokenizers. We add a comparative visualization to chapter 9 (Byte and Character Representations), showing different approaches to grouping bytes into latent tokens.

🔬 Research. Building on the described algorithms, a follow-up on the paper proposes combining SuperBPE’s merging of words into superword tokens with SPLINTER’s morphological templates, allowing sentence-level templates to form superwords from non-adjacent words. Inspired by work on arithmetic, a second follow-up questions why models read and write with the same tokenizer and proposes experiments that separate the two.

💻 Coding. Back to BPE: we put the code for BPE provided in the paper to the test. On the variants: PickyBPE reimplements and compares PickyBPE vs. BPE, exploring the “junk” tokens pruning threshold. BPE-Dropout explores the rate of merge skipping. Greedy vs. Shortest-Path Tokenization tackles the survey’s comparison of MaxMatch and PathPiece. While the paper gives an example of MaxMatch using more tokens, an experiment on a synthetic vocabulary shows this happens in about 25% of tested strings.

🔭 Scouting. Papers challenging the survey raise questions about the bits-per-byte metric for comparing tokenizers. After tokenization, attention and MLP layers relate tokenized fragments back to full words. Two posts look beyond fixed tokenization: one on how the optimal token size depends on the compute budget, and the other suggesting adaptive tokenization.

📣 Communication. To be updated soon
entry.summary: Our focus points from an extensive survey on tokenization
